title: KV Cache Eviction & Paging Deep Dive - Horizon Financial
summary: Deep dive on KV cache architecture and troubleshooting. Horizon seeing intermittent cache evictions and paging to disk for long-context workloads (32k-64k). Discussed eviction policies, memory budgeting, prefix reuse, paging strategies (SSD vs network store), monitoring signals, and short-term mitigations vs longer-term architecture options.
topics: Prefix reuse and cache hit rate
action_items: Samir (SE) - share kv-hit/eviction log parser and sample grafana dashboard - 2025-08-25
Maria (customer) - run Redwood perf harness with 32 concurrent sessions and sample conversation, upload logs to shared S3 link - 2025-08-28
Avery (AE) - send security doc & on-prem deployment note about SSD paging and KMS considerations - 2025-08-24
Leo (customer) - confirm disk policy for on-prem nodes (allow local SSD for paging?) and firewall for Redwood private connector - 2025-08-29
next_steps: Run targeted benchmark to reproduce eviction spike (SE provides harness)
Share KV cache metrics (kv_cache_size, kv_cache_hits, evictions_per_min, page_in/out) via shared dashboard
Agree on mitigation: temporary increase per-worker KV limit + tweak eviction to LFU for prefix-heavy workloads
Schedule follow-up tech sync in one week to review logs and results
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: thanks everyone for joining, i'll kick us off. this is a technical deep dive around the kv cache evictions and paging behavior you're seeing. Samir from our se team is here.
[00:12] Maria Gonzalez: hi thanks, we appreciate it. to summarize, when we run long-context conversations (~32k to 64k tokens) we see intermittent latency spikes and occasional failures; the app logs show 'kv cache evicted' and then a bunch of page-in io, which kills our p99.
[00:28] Samir Patel: ok got it. before we jump in can you share the deployment mode? hosted, dedicated, or private?
[00:34] Leo Rivers: we're on private, datacenter nodes behind our VPC peering. we have 4 workers per model group, each with 48GB GPU memory and 128GB host ram, and we allowed local 500GB SSD for caching but ops has it restricted for security reasons.
[00:49] Priya Kapoor: yeah about that, we have to follow disk encryption + KMS rules; we prefer not to have unencrypted swap on host, so we were hoping for network-backed paging if needed.
[00:58] Samir Patel: makes sense. quick lay of the land: our runtime keeps KV cache per worker (kv for past keys/values) to accelerate autoregressive generation. when context > certain length or many concurrent streams, cache memory can saturate and the runtime either evicts keys (by policy) or spills pages to disk. eviction hurts future latency; paging causes high I/O latency spikes.
[01:20] Maria Gonzalez: can you explain eviction policy differences? we saw references to LRU and LFU in the docs but not sure which is best for our prefix reuse case.
[01:29] Samir Patel: sure. LRU evicts based on recent use, LFU evicts rarely used entries. for chat-like flows with strong prefix reuse (same system and assistant prompts) LFU often retains those hot prefixes better. LRU can thrash if you have lots of interleaved sessions.
[01:40] Speaker 2: and also the runtime has an adaptive policy we call "hotset retention" which can be tuned; but note the naming in the logs can appear as 'kv-evict' or 'kv-evic' because of transcriber quirks.
[01:53] Maria Gonzalez: ok that aligns; our traffic is session-based with many users reusing system prompt templates, so i'd expect hot prefixes.
[02:00] Samir Patel: then LFU or a hybrid (freq-weighted-LRU) is recommended. also bumping per-worker kv capacity helps if memory available. question: are you seeing evictions evenly or bursty with spikes?
[02:12] Leo Rivers: mostly bursty during batch imports and also when many long conversations hit simultaneously. sometimes we see a steady drip of evictions after a large import job.
[02:20] Samir Patel: import jobs are tricky because they can fill the cache with one-off prefixes. two quick mitigations: 1) isolate import traffic to separate pool or throttle it, 2) pre-warm or pin hot prefixes so they don't get evicted.
[02:33] Maria Gonzalez: how do we pin prefixes?
[02:36] Samir Patel: we support a pin API in the runtime that marks keys as protected from eviction up to a configured percentage of cache. it's in the private deploy notes, i'll share the doc.
[02:45] Avery Chen: (AE) we'll include that in the follow-up email.
[02:48] Maria Gonzalez: regarding paging - when it spills to disk, is it local SSD or remote? we can't do unencrypted local disks easily.
[02:55] Samir Patel: runtime supports multiple spill backends: local encrypted SSD (lowest latency), network object store with caching layer, and an in-memory LRU with compaction. Network store will have higher lat but can be encrypted and integrate with your KMS. the key is the page in/out latency and throughput. if page-in is 30-200ms you will see p99 jumps.
[03:12] Tom (data scientist): are we talking about OS-level swap or runtime-level paging?
[03:16] Samir Patel: runtime-level paging of KV entries. we avoid OS swap because it's unpredictable. we page structured kv shards with an index, that lets us fetch only needed rows.
[03:25] Maria Gonzalez: do we have instrumentation to show page_in/page_out events?
[03:28] Samir Patel: yes, our metrics expose kv_cache_hit_ratio, evictions_per_min, page_in_ms_p50, page_in_ms_p99, page_out_bytes, and kv_cache_memory_bytes. If you can share those graphs we can correlate.
[03:40] Maria Gonzalez: we'll pull the grafana panels.
[03:42] Leo Rivers: a weird thing: when we turn on quantization (4-bit) for the model weights to reduce gpu memory, we see more aggressive evictions. any reason?
[03:50] Samir Patel: couple possibilities: quantized models tend to increase CPU-side memory because we store additional structures (dequant tables, packing state), also the runtime may allocate different kv encodings for lower-bit kernels. short answer: quantization can change host memory patterns; we should measure kv_cache_memory_bytes pre/post quant.
[04:07] Maria Gonzalez: ok noted. another symptom: we see a lot of small evictions (single prefixes) which then get refetched, causing p99 blips; is there a way to batch refetches?
[04:17] Samir Patel: yes, runtime supports asynchronous prefetch when it detects correlated misses. it's disabled at default because it can increase bandwidth. you can enable 'prefetch_hot_prefixes' with a threshold; that will group page-ins. also please check your batching settings: huge batching can cause many different KV entries to be touched simultaneously which increases working set.
[04:34] Maria Gonzalez: our batch size is auto, often high for throughput. is there a recommended pattern for long-context chat?
[04:40] Samir Patel: for long-context low-latency chat we recommend smaller batch sizes (2-8) and use the prefix-reuse optimization; for throughput-first batched inference, you accept larger working set and need more KV capacity.
[04:52] Priya Kapoor: from security perspective we need any local SSD to be encrypted and tied to our KMS; does Redwood support that for private deployments?
[04:58] Samir Patel: yes, we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for disk encryption. for on-prem we also support an option to spill to a network store that sits in your VPC with TLS + encrypted at rest. we'll include the architecture note in the security doc.
[05:12] Avery Chen: quick check on logs: can you paste a snippet of a typical eviction log?
[05:16] Maria Gonzalez: sure - "2025-08-10T13:22:44Z INFO kv-evict key=prefix_7c9 count=1 reason=mem_pressure worker=3". sometimes the key name is truncated in logs.
[05:29] Samir Patel: that looks like a mem_pressure eviction. we want to see if the key counts are many unique keys or the same key repeatedly evicted. kv_cache_hit_ratio over time will tell us that.
[05:40] Maria Gonzalez: what's your view on shared vs per-worker cache? we're per-worker now which duplicates hot prefixes across workers. would a shared process-level cache help?
[05:49] Samir Patel: tradeoffs: per-worker cache isolates memory and avoids cross-worker locking, but duplicates hot data. shared cache reduces duplication but adds contention & complexity. for on-prem with plenty of host RAM, per-worker with larger capacity is simplest. We also support a local dedupe layer that keeps references instead of full copies - that's a config we can enable in the runtime.
[06:10] Leo Rivers: the dedupe option sounds interesting, what are the limits?
[06:14] Samir Patel: it saves about 30-50% of host memory for repeated prefixes at the cost of a small CPU and pointer indirection overhead. works best when prefixes are identical across sessions.
[06:25] Maria Gonzalez: can it be enabled on the fly?
[06:27] Samir Patel: yes via rollout flag for the pool. we can enable in staging first.
[06:31] Tom (data scientist): about monitoring - any recommended alerts to catch eviction-caused regressions before customer impact?
[06:36] Samir Patel: alert on sustained evictions_per_min > X (we typically use 10/min as a starting threshold for small pools), sharp drops in kv_cache_hit_ratio, and page_in_ms_p99 > 50ms. pair that with application-level p99 latency alerts.
[06:50] Maria Gonzalez: you mentioned pre-warm - how to do that for hundreds of prefixes?
[06:55] Samir Patel: we have a prewarm job that takes a list of prefixes and runs minimal forward passes to load KV into cache; it's rate-limited. for many prefixes you can do phased warm-ups during off-peak.
[07:05] Avery Chen: practical steps we recommend today: 1) run the perf harness to reproduce, 2) increase per-worker kv_budget if host ram allows, 3) switch eviction to LFU/hybrid and enable prefix pinning for top N system prompts, 4) enable prefetching with a conservative threshold, 5) if disk is allowed, use encrypted local SSD for spill, else use network store with higher latency and tune alerts.
[07:28] Maria Gonzalez: sounds good. curious about 'paging to network store' numbers - what p99s are typical?
[07:33] Samir Patel: network store p99 often 50-200ms depending on topology; local SSD p99 is typically 5-20ms. those numbers directly add to generation p99 when page-in blocks token generation.
[07:46] Speaker 3: (crosstalk) also note that model variants that use different attention kernels change how many KV entries are created per token, so a model change can increase working set even if token count identical.
[07:58] Maria Gonzalez: is there anything about kv shard sizing we should know?
[08:02] Samir Patel: shards are block-aligned; if you choose very small shard sizes you increase metadata overhead; large shards can cause hot keys to bring in more unrelated rows. default is a balanced 4MB shard for your scale.
[08:15] Maria Gonzalez: ok. we'll check our shard config.
[08:18] Tom: you mentioned batching increases working set. is it worth having mixed pool types for latency vs throughput?
[08:23] Samir Patel: yes, many customers run two pools: a low-latency pool with small batch size, pinned prefixes, larger per-worker KV, and a throughput pool optimized for cost. traffic routing can send interactive users to low-latency pool and background jobs to throughput pool.
[08:39] Leo Rivers: we have regulatory constraints around storing any user prompts on disk for longer than 7 days; will that affect the LRU/LFU decisions?
[08:46] Priya Kapoor: yes retention policies must be honored; we need eviction to remove user-specific keys older than 7 days and not persist them to any long-term object store.
[08:54] Samir Patel: that's doable. the runtime supports retention policies per key namespace and will not spill certain namespaces to persistent stores. we'll document the config.
[09:02] Maria Gonzalez: a quick note - our logs show many small keys named like 'session-uuid-prefix-...'; maybe we should canonicalize keys to reduce uniqueness?
[09:10] Samir Patel: canonicalization is a big win. if you can map session-specific keys to stable prefix ids where appropriate you'll get much higher cache hit rates.
[09:18] Maria Gonzalez: we'll look into canonicalization.
[09:21] Avery Chen: ok let's move to concrete debugging steps - Samir, what traces/logs do you need?
[09:25] Samir Patel: the top items: per-worker kv_cache_memory_bytes over time, kv_cache_hit_ratio, evictions_per_min with key samples, page_in_ms p50/p99, page_in_bytes, and any worker OOM or kernel logs. also request IDs around p99 incidents.
[09:38] Maria Gonzalez: we can produce those. do you have a script to parse the evictions and collate hot keys?
[09:43] Samir Patel: yes i'll share a parser that groups evictions by key pattern and shows churn; that will help identify whether it's a few hot keys cycling or wide cardinality.
[09:51] Tom: one more thing - sometimes our sessions include long system prompts (several KB). does that impact KV size dramatically?
[09:57] Samir Patel: yes system prompts are stored in KV and large system context increases working set; consider compressing system prompts or using reference ids (store the full text in an external secure store and reference it in prompt) to reduce KV footprint.
[10:12] Maria Gonzalez: interesting. could we put large static docs in an external store and reference them?
[10:15] Samir Patel: absolutely, that's a common pattern. the runtime has hooks to fetch external context during generation as well.
[10:22] Avery Chen: we've hit 10 minutes of core technical Q&A, want to fast-forward to the action plan and open items?
[10:28] Maria Gonzalez: yes please.
[10:30] Samir Patel: recap: probable root causes - 1) import jobs and large batch patterns inflating working set, 2) per-worker kv_budget too low for your mix, 3) quantization changed host memory layout, 4) no prefix pinning/canonicalization. Recommended immediate mitigations: increase kv_budget, switch to LFU/hybrid, pin top prefixes, run prewarm. Medium term: consider dedupe layer or shared cache and allow encrypted local SSD for paging.
[10:58] Maria Gonzalez: we'll prioritize immediate mitigations and run the perf harness Samir gives.
[11:03] Avery Chen: next steps agreed and action items noted. thanks everyone.
[11:10] Priya Kapoor: we'll loop in compliance on the disk encryption notes.
[11:14] Maria Gonzalez: thanks all. bye.
[11:18] Avery Chen: bye!
